continuity_scope: A three-tale sample from Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, Kinder- und Haus-Märchen, seventh edition / Ausgabe letzter Hand (Göttingen: Dieterich, 1857), volume 1: KHM 15 “Hänsel und Grethel,” KHM 55 “Rumpelstilzchen,” and KHM 69 “Jorinde und Joringel.” Each KHM number is a separate tale continuity; the collection is not treated as a single shared world or character continuity.

coverage_rule: Include only named individual or stable title-designated dramatic characters in the three declared tales: Hänsel and Grethel (KHM 15), Rumpelstilzchen (KHM 55), and Jorinde and Joringel (KHM 69). Generic family roles, the unnamed witch/Erzzauberin, sovereigns, the unnamed miller's daughter, animals, groups of transformed birds, objects, magic, places, and motifs remain dimensions/source terms. The pass is complete only for these five named-character records in these exact tale witnesses.
omissions: All KHM tales other than KHM 15, KHM 55, and KHM 69; the collection's children's legends, annotations, manuscripts, regional variants, translations, and adaptations
All 1812/1815 through 1850 KHM edition states and every post-1857 reprint, retelling, film, game, comic, and other adaptation
Generic roles and unnamed actors in the selected tales, including parents, king/queen, miller/miller's daughter, witch/Erzzauberin, peasant figures, animals, and groups of birds
Objects, places, motifs, magical practices, and divine/diabolic references, which remain terms rather than graph nodes
uncertainties: Kinder- und Haus-Märchen underwent seven materially differing lifetime editions. The 1857 seventh edition is a defined witness, not a neutral reconstruction of oral sources or of the first edition; tale number and title spelling must not be used to collapse other edition states.

Title and translation forms vary. This pass preserves the 1857 German forms “Hänsel und Grethel,” “Rumpelstilzchen,” and “Jorinde und Joringel”; familiar English forms are aliases or orientation only, not replacement witnesses.

The selected tales contain child abandonment under famine, coercion, imprisonment, cannibalistic threat, forced exchange of a child, magical coercion, killing, and violent self-destruction. They are represented descriptively and without treating their outcomes as moral endorsement. No antisemitic wording was identified in this limited three-tale sample; no claim is made about the wider collection.

Terms such as Hexe, Erzzauberin, Jungfrau, and keusch are source-period German narrative language. They receive source-specific, non-equating term records and no mapping to real persons, religions, genders, cultures, or social categories.
evidence_basis: Primary claims use the 1857 German text, with printed KHM number and page range. The Internet Archive supplies a digitized 1857 Dieterich volume; the page-linked German transcription supports precise reading. UNESCO and the Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin supply institutional bibliographic context that the 1857 seventh edition was the final lifetime Ausgabe letzter Hand; scholarly context is used only to explain edition boundaries, not to substitute for the tales.
